subject: Banking
title: Interchange Fees on Every Swipe
description: A micro-lesson that makes Interchange Fees on Every Swipe usable.

hook.text: Every time you swipe a card, the merchant pays 1.5-3% to the bank. US interchange fees exceeded $100 billion in 2022.

buildup.text: The fee is split between the card network, the issuing bank, and the payment processor. The bank gets the largest share.

discovery.text: Interchange fees fund credit card rewards. Banks earn 2% on your purchase and give you back 1% in points.

twist.text: Merchants raise prices to cover interchange fees. Cash customers subsidize card users' rewards without knowing it.

climax.text: Interchange fees are invisible to cardholders but visible in every price tag. You pay whether you use a card or not.

punchline.text: $100 billion in swipe fees. Hidden in every purchase you make.

quiz.question: Who ultimately pays interchange fees?
options: Merchants, who pass the cost to all customers through higher prices

details.summary: Every time you use a debit or credit card, the merchant pays an interchange fee of 1 to 3 percent to your bank. These invisible charges generate over $100 billion annually and are ultimately paid by consumers through higher retail prices.
details.whyItMatters: Interchange fees are the invisible tax on commerce that funds bank rewards programs. Every consumer pays higher prices to cover these fees, but only cardholders who earn rewards get some value back.
takeaways: US interchange fees exceeded $100 billion in 2023
Credit card interchange is typically 1.5-3 percent per transaction
Merchants pass these costs to all consumers through higher prices

faq.question: Who actually pays interchange fees?
faq.answer: Merchants pay the fee directly but pass the cost to consumers through higher prices. Since prices are the same for cash and card customers, cash users effectively subsidize card rewards programs. This transfer is regressive, benefiting wealthier cardholders.

faq.question: Why are interchange fees so controversial?
faq.answer: Merchants argue fees are too high and set by card networks with monopoly power. Banks argue fees fund fraud protection and rewards programs. Regulators have capped debit interchange but credit card interchange remains largely unregulated in the US.
